title: Magenta TV’s Cypriot-Set Thriller ‘Brothers’ Wasn’t Allowed To Shoot In The Country. The Producers Explain Why: “The Reasons Were Political”
full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Magenta TV’s Cypriot-Set Thriller ‘Brothers’ Wasn’t Allowed To Shoot In The Country. The Producers Explain Why: “The Reasons Were Political” ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ Trailer: More Plot Details Emerge In Latest Look At Fincher-Tarantino-Pitt Team-Up Oscar Micheaux Film And Media Institute To Launch Theatrical Roadshow Program For Independent Filmmakers View All November 7, 2026 6:43am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Magenta TV’s Brothers. Magenta TV. Nicosia, the capital of Cyprus, is at the center of Brothers, the new 6-part series by Simon Farmakas, but producers Fenia Cossovitsa and Alexandra Hoesdorff revealed this afternoon during a panel in Thessaloniki that the show couldn’t shoot in the city. Cossovitsa and Hoesdorff were joined on the panel by Faye Tsitsipi, Deputy Director of Content Management at MagentaTV, which will broadcast the series in Greece. The show follows an unorthodox Turkish Cypriot and a hard-headed Greek Cypriot detective who unexpectedly join forces with a European bank auditor in her fight to bring down a politically corrupt network. Related Stories News Thessaloniki: Walter Thompson-Hernández's 'If I Go Will They Miss Me' Among Titles Set For International Competition News Thessaloniki: Adaptation Of Ioanna Karystiani's 'Swell' Among 2026 Agora Works In Progress Titles The series was shot across several European countries, including Germany, Luxembourg, and Greece, but not Cyprus. When asked why the production was spread so widely across Europe, Farmakas told the audience in Thessaloniki that the producers were “forced” to do so on political grounds. Watch on Deadline “In August 2025, we submitted the project to the Ministry of Culture in Cyprus for the equivalent of a cash rebate. It was five or six months of long discussions explaining what the project would be,” she said. Hoesdorff added: “We had a meeting in Cannes, and we had a Zoom call with everyone. They had read the presentation and the first episode, so they knew what the project was about. That’s very important.” Cossovitsa continued to say that “in December 2025, we were told—and it’s important to say this was communicated verbally, not in writing—that they couldn’t commit to the project. This happened just before we started production.” Cossovitsa said the series was already in pre-production. She said reasons the Ministry of Culture in Cyprus turned the project down were “political, obviously.” Cossovitsa continued to suggest that the Cypriot government was unwilling to support a project that predominantly represented Turkish Cypriots. “You can’t make people disappear,” she said. “You can’t pretend that, on the other side of the no man’s land, there isn’t the Turkish-occupied part. You can’t say there are no Turkish detectives. You can’t leave out the Turkish flag, because when you go to Nicosia, it’s there. We couldn’t make them disappear. That was the request.” Hoesdorff said the decision from the Cypriot government put the production in a “very difficult situation” financially. “One has to understand that Cyprus has very high tax credits. Moving everything to Greece made a huge logistical and financial difference,” she said. “So we had to become very creative—more creative than usual—to solve the huge gap we suddenly faced.” Brothers is currently in post. Farmakas is the showrunner. His previous credits include Sunrise in Kimmeria (2018). Tsitsipi said Brothers will likely land on MagentaTV in the next year. title: Paul Howard Dies: Son Of Three Stooges’ Moe Howard, Keeper Of The Flame Was 91
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘The End Of Oak Street’ Gets HBO Max Streaming Release Date ‘Buena Vista Social Club’ Sets Broadway Closing; West End Production Announced For 2027 Kimmarie Johnson Dies: ‘Beverly Hills, 90210’ & ‘Dude, Where’s My Car?’ Actor Was 50 View All November 7, 2026 6:34am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Moe Howard, Paul Howard circa 1940s Courtesy C3 Entertainment Paul Howard , the only son of The Three Stooges ‘ Moe Howard and the last surviving son of the comedy team’s classic line up – Moe, brothers Curly and Shemp, and Larry Fine – died this week. He was 91. The death was confirmed by a spokesperson for C3 Entertainment, the owner of The Three Stooges license and brand. An exact date or cause of death was not specified. Howard, who lived on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, had acted as a guardian of his father’s legacy, often interacting with fans over the years and, in the words of C3, providing “a unique, firsthand view of the man behind the iconic bowl cut and timeless slapstick comedy.” Related Stories News Kimmarie Johnson Dies: 'Beverly Hills, 90210' & 'Dude, Where's My Car?' Actor Was 50 News More Details Revealed About 'Ellen DeGeneres Show' EP Matthew Wright's Sudden Death Both Moe Howard and Larry Fine died in 1975; Moe’s brothers Shemp and Curly died in 1955 and 1952, respectively. Watch on Deadline “He connected directly with generations of The Three Stooges fans at various conventions and events over the years, sharing personal stories, family memories, and insights into the life of Moe Howard and the Stooges’ enduring impact on American pop culture,” the announcement stated. In 2015, Paul Howard hosted an acclaimed 9-part docuseries Hey Moe, Hey Dad! , a series that served as an intimate, definitive tribute to the legacy of The Three Stooges, featuring rare archival footage, personal family accounts, and interviews with the families of Moe Howard, Larry Fine, Curly Howard, Shemp Howard, and latter Stooge Curly Joe DeRita, as well as interviews with well-known celebrity fans including Whoopi Goldberg, Billy West, and Leonard Maltin. The docuseries is available on The Three Stooges+ YouTube channel. Moe Howard, Larry Fine, Curly Howard, 1936 Everett Collection The Three Stooges, of course, were the beloved comedy troupe active from the early 1920s through 1970 who starred in nearly 200 film shorts that featured their slapstick, cartoonishly violent humor. Moe Howard and Larry Fine were part of the act throughout its existence, with either of Howard’s brothers Samuel “Shemp” Howard and Jerome “Curly” Howard taking the role of third stooge at various times during the act’s prime years. After the deaths of Shemp and Curly in the 1950s, comics Joe Besser and “Curly Joe” DeRita filled in during the 1960s. The C3 statement concluded, Paul Howard’s “devotion to preserving his family’s history leaves a lasting imprint on the global Stooges community. He will be remembered fondly for his dedication to honoring his father’s memory and the joy he brought to fans worldwide.” Howard is survived by daughter Jennifer and nephew Jeffrey. ‘Godzilla’ Stalks $30M-$33M Domestic Bow, Best Ever For Foreign-Language Pic ‘Grey’s’ Spinoff Pushed To 2027-28; Shoot Moves To N.M. title: How A Mistake In Warner Bros. Contracts Helped Eleven Film & Jack Thorne Land ‘Lord Of The Flies’ TV Rights — Thessaloniki
full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Magenta TV’s Cypriot-Set Thriller ‘Brothers’ Wasn’t Allowed To Shoot In The Country. The Producers Explain Why: “The Reasons Were Political” ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ Trailer: More Plot Details Emerge In Latest Look At Fincher-Tarantino-Pitt Team-Up Oscar Micheaux Film And Media Institute To Launch Theatrical Roadshow Program For Independent Filmmakers View All November 7, 2026 3:40am Add us as a Google Preferred Source David McKenna as Piggy in 'Lord of the Flies' BBC/Eleven/Lisa Tomasetti “It’s the only thing I’ve ever done that I’d describe, without feeling embarrassed, as hard work,” Joel Wilson of Eleven Film said when discussing his role as an executive producer on Jack Thorne’s Lord of the Flies adaptation. Wilson was speaking on a panel at the Thessaloniki Film Festival, where the series is screening this weekend. Wilson added: “It was genuinely physically tough and psychologically rigorous. But the creative process was the most joyful one I’ve ever been involved in.” Related Stories News Thessaloniki: Walter Thompson-Hernández's 'If I Go Will They Miss Me' Among Titles Set For International Competition News Thessaloniki: Adaptation Of Ioanna Karystiani's 'Swell' Among 2026 Agora Works In Progress Titles The four-part series, based on William Golding’s novel of the same name, launched on the BBC in the UK in February and started streaming on Netflix in the U.S. in May. Adolescence co-creator and Emmy winner Thorne adapted the book for the screen. Wilson told the audience in Thessaloniki that the process began many years earlier, when he unsuccessfully contacted Golding’s estate to enquire about purchasing the Lord of the Flies TV rights. Watch on Deadline “I hadn’t done very much, and they politely told me to come back later,” Wilson joked. “So I did, again and again. Eventually, we made Sex Education , and our reputation had grown since the first time I’d called them.” Wilson added that he later developed a relationship with the agent who owned the stage rights to the book, whom he called “every six months”, and later tipped him off about a potential quirk in the book’s copyright contracts that could open the door for a TV adaptation. “Warner Bros. owned the rights and had tried to remake it several times without success,” Wilson explained. “It was unclear in the original contract whether Warner Bros. owned the film and television rights or only the film rights because the idea of making Lord of the Flies for television wouldn’t have been considered at the time.” Wilson said the Golding family retained the TV rights and, miraculously, around the same time, Thorne, whom he had worked with before, mentioned his interest in adapting the book. “I’d offered him another project he didn’t want to do, and said, ‘If you don’t want to do that, how am I ever going to get you to work with me again?’” Golding said of the conversation he had with Thorne. “He responded, ‘If you can get the rights to Lord of the Flies , I’ll do that.’ It’s one of the only moments in my life I’d genuinely describe as serendipitous. I nearly fell off my chair and said, ‘I’m speaking to the family about it now. Can I email them on Monday with Jack Thorne— Lord of the Flies in the subject line? He said, Absolutely.” Wilson explained that with Thorne attached, the project quickly picked up momentum. “We then pitched it to the BBC. It was the first time this had happened to me, though it seems to happen to everyone else: We went in and said, ‘Jack wants to make Lord of the Flies . Are you in?’ They said, ‘Yes, please,’” Wilson recalled. “There wasn’t even a script, but the vision was very clear, and they greenlit it.” Marc Munden ( The Mark of Cain, National Treasure ) directed the series, with Wilson executive producing alongside his Eleven colleague Jamie Campbell and Thorne. Hans Zimmer provided music for the series, which was nominated for two Emmys. “I think we managed to do exactly what we set out to do: protect the vision Jack and Mark had, which relates so closely to the original novel,” Wilson said of the series. “I’m glad to say Judy, William Golding’s daughter, was delighted with it. That was one of the most important things, because the book was so precious to her.” The 2026 Thessaloniki Film Festival runs until November 15. ‘Godzilla’ Stalks $30M-$33M Domestic Bow, Best Ever For Foreign-Language Pic ‘Grey’s’ Spinoff Pushed To 2027-28; Shoot Moves To N.M. title: PÖFF Stands With Ukraine: A Look at Films Featured at Tallinn Made Despite, and Because of, the War
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All November 7, 2026 3:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'To Live to Die' Courtesy of PÖFF The Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival ( PÖFF ) has been standing with Ukraine and showing solidarity since the 2022 full-scale invasion of the country by Russia, featuring Ukrainian films, showcasing works-in-progress and organizing Ukraine-themed panels in its industry strand Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event. “We are obliged to do everything possible to help and support the Ukrainian film industry at this difficult time, but even more so the Ukrainian people,” PÖFF founder and CEO Tiina Lokk said in 2022. This year, for the 30th anniversary edition of the festival, its PÖFF Standing With Ukraine film showcase is back. “Ukraine is fighting not only for Ukraine, but also for Europe and the democratic world,” Lokk tells THR . ”And so we are going to support Ukraine and stand with Ukraine as long as needed. It is important for Ukraine to remain very visible and to keep its culture. And it is very important for every country.” Related Stories Oscars 2027: Int'l Films in Focus 'Hold Onto Me,' Cyprus' First Oscar Hopeful, Stars a Newcomer and a 'Dogtooth' Actor in a Very Personal Father-Daughter Drama TV 'The Remarried Empress' Sets Disney+ and Hulu Record With Biggest Local Original Launch Ever Marge Liiske, head of the Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event, emphasizes that the industry strand of the Estonian festival also continues to put a spotlight on the war. “We have since the 2022 [full-scale invasion by Russia] very supportive of Ukraine and have always reflected that in our program, both for the festival and the industry events,” she tells THR . She and Triin Tramberg , PÖFF’s new artistic director, highlight that they will always put a spotlight on Ukraine and other countries standing up for important democratic values. “Throughout our program, we’re supporting countries that are fighting for their rights and for their democracy,” Tramberg tells THR . “We also have to understand where we are located. Standing With Ukraine is really important for us as a region, and it speaks to our audiences and our communities, including Ukrainians who live here. It is important to have this moment where they see their own cinema.” PÖFF’s Standing With Ukraine strand this year showcases nine features that are diverse and different. And many also screen in other Tallinn strands, as you can see below. Take a closer look at the films right here. Slava: Shooting With Music Director: Jacqui Morris, David Morris Festival section: Special Screenings ‘Slava: Shooting With Music’ Courtesy of PÖFF Silence the guns and let the music play! This world premiere is about the power of music and culture more broadly. “Sviatoslav Vakarchuk is the lead singer of Okean Elzy, Ukraine’s most successful rock band. He is a former politician and activist who has a PhD in theoretical physics,” reads a synopsis of the film. “Slava has been compared to Bruce Springsteen and Paul McCartney, and his songs are an important part of Ukrainian identity, part of the country’s cultural DNA. He is now channeling his talents to liberate his country.” After playing more than 200 concerts for the troops, he decided to take his band on a worldwide tour to bolster the morale of Ukrainian refugees living abroad. And an international coalition of artists, including Coldplay, stepped up to support the band. Highlights the Synopsis: “Another reason for the tour was to leave a lasting legacy in the minds of the rest of the world of Ukrainian culture – a unique culture Russia has been trying to eradicate for centuries.” Vesna Director: Rostislav Kirpicenko Festival section: Baltic Film Competition ‘Vesna’ Courtesy of PÖFF Honoring the dead becomes dangerous in times of war, as this film shows. In a town in southeastern Ukraine that is occupied by Russian forces, burying the dead has actually been forbidden. The church of a young priest has even been turned into a morgue for executed civilians. But the priest begins to quietly resist, secretly returning the bodies to their families at great personal risk. And in the process, he forms an unlikely bond with an 11-year-old boy who becomes a silent witness to his rebellion. The drama adds a focus on the psychological and emotional warfare beyond the physical battles. “Lithuanian-born Ukrainian director Rostislav Kirpicenko uncovers cynicism, blackmail, and the brutal cruelty of the merciless attackers,” the PÖFF website says about the film. What would you do if you were in the shoes of the locals who face horrible choices – fight back, obey and adapt to the brutal new reality, or even betray? Emphasizes the festival website: “The mightiest impact here is heartbreaking authenticity, showing how Ukrainians are surviving the ongoing occupation.” I Rarely Wake up Dreaming Director: Isabelle Stever Section: Standing With Ukraine ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming’ Courtesy of X Filme Creative Pool War surely can affect love. But how does the transition from peace to warfare – yes, Russia’s full-scale invasion! – affect a queer couple in Ukraine, especially when the geopolitical change comes in parallel with a gender transition? I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming made an impact when it world-premiered at Locarno, leading to conversations between viewers and beyond. You can read our chat with the creators right here. But you really have to watch the film to see how the relationship between Olya and Oleh is put to the test when the gender transition allows the couple to get married, but also stirs up all sorts of personal and national identity struggles. To Die to Live Director: Yuliia Hontaruk Festival section: Doc@PÖFF Baltic Competition ‘To Live to Die’ Courtesy of PÖFF Yuliia Hontaruk’s doc introduces us to three men who have experienced huge change over the course of their lives. In 2014, they had no military experience but volunteered to go to the front line. When they returned home after two years, they tried to find an ordinary life rhythm again. But they just can’t seem to succeed. After all, the war has left its mark on their bodies and minds, which affects their family lives. “It is a brutal truth that is not always easy to capture on film,” the PÖFF summary of the film notes. “And then the men have to go back to war. Their previous experience was merely a preparation for what would happen in February 2022, when Russia launched a full-scale invasion. They are back on the front line, now fully aware of what this does to them.” The filmmaker followed the three men for 12 years, leading to a film whose fragmented feel mirrors the fragmented lives and trauma. Wings Director: Ana Rocha de Sousa Section: Standing With Ukraine ‘Wings’ You can take people out of a war zone. But can you ever really take the war trauma out of their lives? Or in other words: Is living in peace the same as enjoying peace of mind? Wings is a drama, shot in Ukraine and Portugal with creatives from both countries, but it was inspired by the real-life story of a Ukrainian family who fled the war and found refuge in Portugal. If you are interested in a deep dive into the lasting impact and trauma of experiencing war and displacement, plus how there may be a path to finding hope, this one is for you. Living On Director: Nerijus Milerius Festival section: Doc@PÖFF Baltic Competition ‘Living On’ Courtesy of PÖFF Art therapy at a veterans’ theater, yoga sessions, hair salons, para-archery and mountain peaks and much more feature in another Ukraine-focused world premiere coming to PÖFF. Standing with Ukraine is exactly what Lithuanian philosopher and director Nerijus Milerius did when he volunteered to drive cars with medical aid to Ukraine’s front lines. Between August 2024 and June 2026, he documented his experiences on 15 dangerous missions and used the filmed material for his fourth feature. “He records daily life under attack and hears dark humor in Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa, Kherson and other bombed areas where he needed a fixer even to gain access,” reads a Tallinn festival tease for the film. And it highlights: “Milerius captures Ukrainians’ resilience and spirit.” Slava Director: Denis Sobolev Section: Standing With Ukraine ‘Slava’ No, this one is not about the rock star Slava we met earlier but a woman. And the story is much more complex. The political thriller is based on a real-life story and shows Slava and Yaroslav Stetsko launching an information campaign, via media and protests, in the U.S. and Europe in the 1960s. Their message: the KGB and the USSR are the architects of political murder beyond Soviet borders. That makes a trial in Karlsruhe, West Germany, take on a political dimension. Bohdan Stashynsky, a KGB agent, has confessed to killing Stepan Bandera, a controversial far-right Ukrainian politician. But while the case is being framed as a “routine” crime, the activists want to highlight that Moscow is exporting political violence via assassinations abroad. The Kremlin responds with threats. And the activists’ friends become concerned, urging them to soften the rhetoric. To see how it all plays out, you’ll have to watch Slava . Camouflage Director: Mykyta Gibalenko Section: Standing With Ukraine ‘Camouflage’ A clash of identity and war already played a key role in one of the films we discussed earlier. They are also in focus in this movie, which premiered at Venice, but in a different way. Vitaly, 22, studies German and moves from Ukraine to Germany, leaving behind his mother, a teacher shaped by the Soviet era, and his sister. And once in Munich, Vitaly finally feels free to be himself and live the life he wants to lead. But a year later, Russia invades Ukraine. And, as you may have expected, due to the war, his mother and sister have to flee their home and seek refuge with Vitaly in Munich. That’s where they learn about his new identity… Traces Directors: Alisa Kovalenko, Marysia Nikitiuk Section: Best of Docs ‘Traces’ Last, but certainly not least, PÖFF Standing With Ukraine will screen a Ukrainian awards season contender. Silence isn’t always golden. Just listen to the six Ukrainian women who survived sexual violence and torture during the Russian war against Ukraine and speak out in Traces . Iryna Dovhan, a former captive-turned-activist, documents testimonies of women affected by the trauma of war-related violence. And following her work, the film weaves together a portrait of collective trauma while opening space for hope. The film premiered in the Panorama section of the Berlin International Film Festival, winning the program’s best documentary award , and became Ukraine’s submission for the best international feature film Oscar. THR

title: ‘3 Body Problem’ Director Derek Tsang Boards DEA True-Crime Series ‘Group 41’ From Zhang Yimou’s ‘Shadow’ Producer Jonah Greenberg (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Nov 7, 2026 1:50am PT ‘3 Body Problem’ Director Derek Tsang Boards DEA True-Crime Series ‘Group 41’ From Zhang Yimou’s ‘Shadow’ Producer Jonah Greenberg (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘3 Body Problem’ Director Derek Tsang Boards DEA True-Crime Series ‘Group 41’ From Zhang Yimou’s ‘Shadow’ Producer Jonah Greenberg (EXCLUSIVE) 5 hours ago Stephen Chow Told Japan to Stop Aping Kung Fu, Says Boss of Film Fund Behind Kore-eda Hirokazu’s ‘Look Back’ 11 hours ago Why ‘Suits’ Japan Swapped Drugs for Cash: NBCUniversal, TBS Format Chiefs on Localizing Hits at Taiwan Creative Content Fest 12 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images/Salty Pictures “3 Body Problem” and “Better Days” filmmaker Derek Tsang is attached to direct and executive produce “ Group 41 ,” a true-crime drama series about the first Asian-American squad at the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). The project, from Jonah Greenberg ’s Salty Pictures, is at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. The 10-episode series, with 45-minute episodes, opens in New York in 1986. While the DEA has its sights set on Colombian cocaine cartels and the city’s “Five Families” of the Mafia, a scrappy crew of Asian-American agents teams up with a hard-charging Irish prosecutor nicknamed “The Dragon Lady.” Together they form DEA Group 41, which becomes the first squad to chase the No. 4 heroin pouring into the U.S. through a network few had noticed. Related Stories Sundance Hires Tracy Brady as Marketing, Communications Chief Over the next decade, the underfunded unit grows into an elite international task force. Its targets include Johnny Kon, a Hong Kong boss whose billion-dollar triad spans five continents; Johnny “Onionhead” Eng, a brutal Chinatown gangster; and Khun Sa, a warlord in the Golden Triangle with a 20,000-strong narco-army. The show explores immigration, prejudice and what the American Dream costs, with stories from both sides of the law. Greenberg, a former managing director of CAA’s China office whose producing credits include Zhang Yimou’s “Shadow,” wrote the source book with Marc Iserlis and Aidan Swift, who are also producers and writers on the series. Greenberg says shows about present-day law enforcement can be great, but surveillance technology now gives cops the upper hand. “Back in the 1980s when you went undercover, you went deep. And all the bad guys carry guns, and the danger to cops and informants is real,” Greenberg says. The crimes, and the agents who solved them, were largely overlooked at the time, he adds. “It simply wasn’t considered as sexy to work Chinese cases in the 1980s. People were busy watching ‘Miami Vice’ (myself chief among them!) and watching Rudy Giuliani convict the Italian mobsters,” Greenberg says. Neither the media nor even the DEA made Asian cases a priority, according to Greenberg. “So it’s an underdog story. It’s literally the war on drugs we actually won but which no one knows about.” He also sees room for several seasons across the 10-year saga, with Khun Sa looming over the whole show as a Colonel Kurtz-like final target, giving the series what Greenberg calls a “save the best for last” advantage. The source material, a 180-page nonfiction book titled “The Incredible Story of D.E.A. Group 41 & The Rise and Fall of the Asian Heroin Trade,” will be published next year. Greenberg says the team has the trust and cooperation of the real people involved. Taiwan’s Each Other Films, co-founded by co-producer Tiffany Yu-chia Chen, is on board as co-production partner, and former CAA TV co-head Adam Berkowitz of Lenore Entertainment Group serves as executive producer. After seven years of development, the next steps are to find a writer-showrunner and possibly attach cast before pitching to platforms next year. Greenberg says what has kept him with the project is a wish to tell stories about people driven by purpose, pointing to Cathy Palmer and the agents of Group 41, who took apart a heroin pipeline running from Southeast Asia to the U.S. “‘Serpico’ was always a foundational film for me and well, maybe nobody liked the guy, but he lived by a certain code. And that’s what interests me,” he says. At TCCF, the team wants to learn how incentives in Taiwan and elsewhere in the region could offset the budget, and to explore distribution in Asia, so that production, financing and perhaps even distribution are lined up efficiently before pitching to U.S. platforms. title: Davika Hoorne Returning for ‘Inherit’ Sequel, Director Banjong Pisanthanakun Confirms (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Nov 7, 2026 12:59am PT Davika Hoorne Returning for ‘Inherit’ Sequel, Director Banjong Pisanthanakun Confirms (EXCLUSIVE) By Jenny S. Li Plus Icon Jenny S. Li Latest Swiss Labor Exploitation Drama ‘Enjoy Your Stay’ Lands in Indonesia, Directors Hope It Speaks for Migrant Workers 15 hours ago Cristian Mungiu’s Cinematographer Tudor Vladimir Panduru Breaks Down Long Takes on ‘Fjord,’ ‘R.M.N.’ at Jakarta World Cinema Masterclass 3 days ago Jakarta World Cinema Plans to Revive First Feature Competition With International Jury 6 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jakarta World Cinema Banjong Pisanthanakun , the Thai director of horror hits “Shutter” and “Pee Mak,” tells Variety his new psychological horror film “ Inherit ” will get a sequel, with star Davika Hoorne set to return. “Inherit,” a Centrepiece selection at the Toronto Film Festival, where it world premiered in September, is closing the Jakarta World Cinema festival. Pisanthanakun and Hoorne first worked together on 2013 horror-comedy “Pee Mak,” Thailand’s biggest local box office hit of all time. Related Stories Liev Schreiber and Stephen Graham Lead Apple TV's Gripping Serial Killer Thriller 'Nocturne': TV Review Hoorne plays Woranart, a youthful-looking grandmother who moves in with her granddaughter’s wealthy family. The family soon discovers she harbors a centuries-old centipede spirit with sinister designs on the youngest in the household, Oui (Baipor Thitiya Jirapornsilp). Hoorne was Pisanthanakun’s first choice for the immortal grandmother. “The character has to be sexy, beautiful, and funny at the same time. I think of her as a fashion icon, too,” Pisanthanakun tells Variety . “The first image that I have was her wearing a bikini and sunbathing beside the pool, which is very modern. She talks like this [era’s] woman, talking to ChatGPT. She’s a very adaptable girl.” On set, Pisanthanakun advised Hoorne to study Catherine Tramell, Sharon Stone’s character in “Basic Instinct,” and Anthony Hopkins’ Hannibal Lecter in “The Silence of the Lambs.” Hoorne also starred in “A Useful Ghost,” the satirical Thai comedy-thriller that took Cannes’ Critics’ Week Grand Prix in 2025. She regards that film and “Inherit” as her return to cinema. “For movie, I carefully choose the project that I want to do,” Hoorne says. “One project takes around one year of working, so I really have to choose the one I’m gonna live with for such a long time to bring up my soul as an actress. So, trust me, watch it, I pick for you guys already.” Pisanthanakun says that 20 years ago, horror was all about the concept – ghosts in photos or on videotapes – with filmmakers competing over where to make the ghost appear. “Actually, after ‘Shutter’ and ‘Alone,’ there came a time when I really got bored of making horror films; even going to the cinema to watch horror films made me fall asleep right away,” the director says. “After films like ‘Hereditary’ and ‘It Follows’ came out, I felt like there were still other new, refreshing ways to make horror films. The modern horror, especially from the Hollywood side, is now very creative. I think it’s the only genre that still has something creative coming up.” His film “The Medium” was produced by Korean director Na Hong-Jin. “When I made this project with him, he shared his opinion on how the international market would react all the time. I just made this film [the way I normally do]. But he’s gonna give his opinion on how the international audience would perceive it,” Pisanthanakun says. “I want the concepts and the story to be as solid as possible, and I want the atmosphere to be everything. It has to be very unique, and everything has to be like authentic,” he adds. On AI, he says: “I think it’s inevitable in the system, but I think people can use it as long as it’s not violating other people’s rights.” “The Thai film industry right now is not so good – that’s the real pressure because I want this movie to bring Thai audiences back to the cinema,” Pisanthanakun says. “Inherit” opens across Thailand Nov. 19. He adds that public funding for Thai film production is neither robust nor consistent, and only goes to horror. Hoorne has moved into producing girls’ love (GL) titles, a genre of romance stories between women that is popular in Thailand. “It’s gonna be better if we have funding from the other help of the government; that help is the independent themes that can go internationally,” Hoorne says. “When I’m producing a movie or series, it is very hard to find the funding, and it is really hard for Thai films to recruit people for different genres. Because you have to draw people into the cinema, drama or comedy, something that looks small, people tend to wait.” Hoorne has also directed a family short film, “Soap Opera,” which recently wrapped, and will focus on TV series in 2027. Pisanthanakun is leading a Thai-Korean horror co-production. title: AI Filmmaking Platform Core Studio Launches at Taiwan Creative Content Fest With 24 Specialized Agents
full_text: × Nov 7, 2026 12:19am PT AI Filmmaking Platform Core Studio Launches at Taiwan Creative Content Fest With 24 Specialized Agents By Lin Ying-Hsuan Plus Icon Lin Ying-Hsuan Latest Taiwan’s Chunghwa Telecom Unveils 10 Content Investments, From ‘Gunshot’ to ‘Call of Lobster’ 12 hours ago Chang Chen Urges Emerging Taiwanese Actors to ‘Be Like Water’ at Taiwan Creative Content Fest Golden Horse Showcase 12 hours ago Taiwan Audience Study Highlights Cross-Platform IP Opportunities as AI Raises New Risks for Content Industry 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source imCore Corp. Taiwanese technology company imCore Corp. launched Core Studio , an AI filmmaking platform that aims to cover the full production process, from script development and storyboarding to image generation, editing and color grading, at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei on Saturday. Built by a Taiwanese team with roots in animation and visual effects, the platform runs on its own in-house image-generation model and also works with outside generative AI models. It follows standard filmmaking workflows, so creators can handle several stages of production in one place instead of switching between tools. Related Stories Liev Schreiber and Stephen Graham Lead Apple TV's Gripping Serial Killer Thriller 'Nocturne': TV Review Guests at the launch included Erica Wang, CEO of TCCF organizer the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA), along with representatives from the Taipei Film Commission and imCore’s strategic partners, filmmakers and AI industry professionals. “Our team understands that professional creators need more than just image-generation tools. They need a comprehensive solution that can genuinely integrate into their production workflows,” said Charles Lee, founder and CEO of imCore Corp. and founder of TWR Entertainment. “Core Studio was developed around the needs of frontline film professionals, transforming years of production expertise into an AI-powered platform that provides more comprehensive creative support for filmmakers.” The platform’s main draw is a set of more than 24 specialized AI agents that act as a virtual production crew, handling story development, asset generation, visual effects, editing and color grading. imCore pitches them as a way to lower the technical hurdles of AI-assisted filmmaking. For pre-production, Core Studio’s Story Atlas tool breaks an imported script into scenes, shots and storyboards. It also sets up character designs, costumes, props and voice profiles so they stay consistent from one sequence to the next. Every AI-generated output comes with a record of the models, prompts, parameters, costs and human review results behind it. Production teams can use it to track creative decisions and keep an eye on budgets. The platform also includes Real Engine, which combines three image-processing tools: Real Video, Real HDR and Real Revive. They sharpen image detail, raise color depth from 8-bit to 16-bit and fix blown-out highlights in AI-generated footage. A cloud workspace with real-time communication, version control and access management lets teams in different countries work on the same project. Creators of four AI-assisted projects presented their work at the launch, among them Jerry Zhou, the creator of “God Being.” “There are many agents on the editing page that can help with sound effects. title: ‘Triplets of Belleville’ Director Sylvain Chomet Fires Back at AI Accusations Over Dior Film Featuring Robert Pattinson’s Voice: ‘Everything Was Drawn by Hand’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Nov 7, 2026 12:12am PT ‘Triplets of Belleville’ Director Sylvain Chomet Fires Back at AI Accusations Over Dior Film Featuring Robert Pattinson’s Voice: ‘Everything Was Drawn by Hand’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest ‘Triplets of Belleville’ Director Sylvain Chomet Fires Back at AI Accusations Over Dior Film Featuring Robert Pattinson’s Voice: ‘Everything Was Drawn by Hand’ (EXCLUSIVE) 7 hours ago ‘You Can See Everything’ Sparks Frenzy in Europe as Screenings Sell Out and Anticipation Soars: ‘People Are Just Desperate to See It’ 22 hours ago Paris Creator Week Aims to Become the Cannes of the Creator Economy as New Study Forecasts $1.2 Trillion Global Market 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Dior French animation filmmaker Sylvain Chomet, the four-time Oscar nominee behind “The Triplets of Belleville” and “The Illusionist,” is pushing back against accusations that generative AI was used to create his animated short for Dior featuring a voice cast led by Robert Pattinson , Rihanna, Josh O’Connor, LaKeith Stanfield, Louis Garrel and Camille Cottin. The whimsical six-minute film, “Christian Dior’s Night in Color,” produced by Aton Soumache (“The Little Prince”), has sparked controversy online, where some viewers have pointed to apparent visual glitches, including a character with six fingers, as evidence of AI-generated animation. Related Stories Liev Schreiber and Stephen Graham Lead Apple TV's Gripping Serial Killer Thriller 'Nocturne': TV Review The controversy flared because Dior positioned “Night in Color” as a celebration of traditional craftsmanship to launch its 2026 holiday season, drawing parallels between Chomet’s hand-drawn animation and the meticulous work of the house’s couture ateliers. But Chomet and Soumache tell Variety that the film was created using traditional 2D animation techniques, with the characters, backgrounds and key poses drawn by artists. While they acknowledge using automated interpolation to generate some of the intermediate frames that make movement fluid, the pair insists that generative AI was never used to create the artwork. “Some people are claiming Sylvain was contacted two weeks ago and that the entire film was made with generative AI, without a single drawing, but the reality is that this film took seven months to make and it was entirely drawn by artists,” says Soumache, adding that film employed roughly 20 people, including six animators, alongside storyboard artists, designers, background artists, compositors and editors. “We used an automated interpolation system for a very small part of the process, but the film itself is traditional 2D animation,” says the French producer. Chomet, whose latest film “A Magnificent Life” world premiered at last year’s Cannes and was distributed theatrically by Sony Pictures Classics, explains that the interpolation tool was only used to help create the in-between frames on “Christian Dior’s Night in Color.” “It’s a way of automating the repetitive, mechanical part of animation, not the creative work,” he says. The filmmaker says the accusations are particularly ironic given how committed he has been to traditional animation despite pressures to branch into CGI after the huge success of “Toy Story.” “Before I made ‘The Triplets of Belleville,’ it was the era of ‘Toy Story.’ I remember Disney declaring that traditional 2D animation was dead and that everything would be CGI, but I decided to continue making hand-drawn films,” Chomet says. “That’s why I find it so strange that people are attacking me today. I’ve remained faithful to drawing throughout my career. At the same time, I’m going to use the tools that technology offers us.” The film draws on several chapters of Dior’s history, including the couturier’s friendship with Marlene Dietrich, his ties to Hollywood and the creation of the iconic Junon gown in 1949. It also takes inspiration from one of the earliest ideas behind Dior creative director Jonathan Anderson’s Cruise 2027 collection: cinema’s transition from black-and-white to Technicolor. The story imagines Dietrich in Los Angeles, preparing to shoot a movie when the director suddenly decides to film in color. An urgent call is placed to Paris requesting a colorful Dior gown for the actress, sending Christian Dior and his team of seamstresses into a race against the clock. Pattinson narrates the film, while Garrel voices Christian Dior and Cottin plays Dietrich. O’Connor voices a talking chair, Rihanna portrays Dior’s lucky star, and Stanfield plays the Hollywood director. Nine d’Urso, Nadia Tereszkiewicz and Greta Lee voice the three bees. Soumache, whose credits include the Cesar-winning “The Little Prince,” has spent much of his career working in CGI before returning to traditional animation with films including Joann Sfar’s “Little Vampire” and more recently “A Magnificent Life,” a biopic of late celebrated French novelist and filmmaker Marcel Pagnol. “Sylvain and I have been championing traditional 2D animation for such a long time, and Dior came to us because they wanted Sylvain’s very distinctive drawing style,” says the producer whose track record also includes the blockbuster French IP “Miraculous Ladybug.” Chomet explains that the production process on the Dior short was rooted in drawing, even if artists now use digital tablets rather than paper. “But we’re still drawing by hand, it’s just done digitally,” he said, adding that he found it frustrating to work on graphic tablets and planned to “go back to pencil and paper because (he loves) having original drawings.” “I design the characters, we create the storyboards, the backgrounds, the colors. The entire creative process is exactly the same as when I started making animated films. What has changed is the technology,” he said. Chomet also addresses the apparent six-fingered hands that have fueled speculation online. “It’s a movement where the hand is spread out like a fan. In that kind of drawing, you might see six or seven fingers because you’re trying to convey movement,” he says. He argues that he’s seen much worse mistakes in traditional animation. “I’ve seen a character turn his head and suddenly his nose changes shape completely over five frames. These things happen.” The short was conceived as part of a broader collaboration with Dior, with Anderson originating the idea and Martin Latham helping develop the screenplay. “I worked particularly closely with Martin. We developed the script together and then presented ideas for the storyboard, the story and the characters. There was a lot of back-and-forth,” Chomet says. The collaboration also extended beyond the screen, with Chomet’s illustrations inspiring Dior’s holiday collections and boutique windows around the world. “Dior needed to see the designs quite early because they were simultaneously developing the Christmas window displays and physical objects,” says Soumache. “Many of Dior’s windows are based directly on Sylvain’s drawings. They created physical versions of the characters and objects from the film.” Chomet describes Disney’s 1961 classic “One Hundred and One Dalmatians” as his “madeleine de Proust,” the film he keeps coming back to. “Whenever I make a film, I ask myself whether it has that poetry, that beauty of drawing,” he says. “We can tell very different stories from the ones Disney was telling at the time, but we can still preserve that beauty. That’s what I’ve always tried to do, using technology to maintain something traditional.” Along with showcasing France’s vibrant animation talent pool, the short film also reflects Anderson’s love for hand-drawn animation. While at Loewe, he collaborated with Japan’s Studio Ghibli on three collections. title: Toei CEO Fumio Yoshimura Talks Global Expansion, GenAI Adoption & Entry Into Games
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz ‘The Remarried Empress’ Sets Disney+ Record As Most Viewed Local Original Launch Ever ‘Dune’ Star Chang Chen Introduces Six Rising Taiwanese Actors In Golden Horse & TCCF Showcase Weta FX CEO Daniel Seah Unpacks TAICCA Partnership: “Taiwan Has Creative Talent, Technology & Government Support” View All November 6, 2026 11:55pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Toei CEO Fumio Yoshimura speaks at TCCF TAICCA Fumio Yoshimura, CEO of Japan’s Toei Co, explained how the studio is working with local partners to globalize its long-established IP, as well as innovating in areas including GenAI and gaming, in a keynote Forum session at Taiwan Creative Content Fest ( TCCF ). In 2023, the 75-year-old studio launched an ambitious $2BN ‘Toei New Wave’ plan to boost its international revenue’s share of total income from 30% to 50% by 2033, which included upgrades to its studio facilities in Tokyo and Kyoto. Since then the company has embarked on several international co-productions and partnerships, started exploring GenAI technology and moved into production of games. Related Stories News 'Dune' Star Chang Chen Introduces Six Rising Taiwanese Actors In Golden Horse & TCCF Showcase News Weta FX CEO Daniel Seah Unpacks TAICCA Partnership: "Taiwan Has Creative Talent, Technology & Government Support" Yoshimura started the session by explaining how the company has been introducing its popular IP to international markets. The latest series in one of its oldest franchises, Kamen Rider Zetz , is currently streaming in Taiwan and other international markets, with India a particular focus. Watch on Deadline “In 2025, we held an event to introduce Kamen Rider to India consumers. We got a very good response and signed a contract with a Disney affiliate to distribute the content. Due to its population size and the growth of its middle-class, we see India as a promising market,” Yoshimura said. Kamen Rider was one of the first franchises that Toei globalized, working with U.S. partners to produce an English-language verskon, Mighty Morphin Power Rangers , more than 30 years ago, with the franchise now handled by toymaker Hasbro. Both the Kamen Rider and Power Rangers franchises have been extended to toys, merchandising and live events. In other IP extensions, Toei recently teamed with Sony’s Anyplex Inc and Godzilla VFX house Shriogumi Inc to launch a Kamen Rider anime label. Other recent localization efforts include the Voltes 5 franchise, which was first launched as an anime in Japan in 1977 and became a cultural phenomenon in the Philippines where its themes of resistance against a repressive empire got it banned by the Marcos regime. In 2023, Philippines broadcaster GMA produced a live-action remake, Voltes V: Legacy , which became a ratings hit in the Philippines and also aired in Japan. “Simply exporting content limits its reach, so in order to break through constraints, we are producing remakes and localisations,” Yoshimura explained. After getting started with remakes, Yoshimura said the studio is now also working on local productions based on original stories: “We’re developing local content from scratch, working with local talent to release locally and then sell globally. We believe this local first model will generate more sustainable long-term revenue than the traditional export model.” Among recent productions, Toei worked with Taiwan’s Lou Lou Film Studio on Dear Stranger , directed by Tetsuya Mariko and starring Hidetoshi Nishijima and Gwei Lun-mei, which screened on the festival circuit last year. More recently, the company worked with Taiwan’s Wowing Entertainment Group on horror film The Rope Curse 4: Kuntilanak , directed by Liao Shih-Han and starring Lee Kang-sheng. Yoshimura identified Taiwan as another key market for Toei’s global expansion, due to cultural similarities and the popularity of Japanese IP in Taiwan. “Data shows that Japanese films had a 26% share of Taiwan’s box office last year, the second highest share after Hollywood with 41%,” Yoshimura said. “Taiwanese audiences have a strong interest in Japanese content.” Toei has also partnered with Thailand’s M Studio on a slate of Thai-language remakes and local features, and is currently working with both M Studio and Korea’s Showbox on a horror feature based on Japanese manga The Long Hair In The Attic , by artist Junji Ito. The studio has also stepped into assisting the growing number of international productions now shooting in Japan, encouraged by Japan’s incentives scheme, including U.S. indie action thriller Iris, created by and starring Dani Swan ( The Matrix Resurrections ). In addition to providing facilities, Toei helped with casting for the film and assisted on the incentives application. On the tech front, Yoshimura explained that the company is expanding the Virtual Production and motion capture facilities at its studios in Tokyo and Kyoto and also starting to use AI in workflows. “We’re also experimenting with GenAI image generation,” Yoshimura said. “The Toei team is performing tests on practical AI applications daily; building tools to assist junior producers in estimating production budgets, and using AI in background artwork. However we believe human creativity remains the core of everything we do.” Microdrama is another area that Toei has stepped into – producing Everyday Host Club , a 24×3-minute anime series, and a 30-episode short-form vertical drama, Meshimori Onna , made for smartphone screens. Gaming is another new area for Toei as it explores how to expand its IP across borders and formats. “Gaming is a global entertainment medium and delivering games to users worldwide aligns perfectly with our global expansion strategy,” Yoshimura said. Toei plans to launch its first game, Hino , developed by UnGloom Studio, in spring 2027, followed by Debug – Nephemee and Killa later next year. All the games will be distributed across platforms and consoles including Steam, Nintendo and Xbox. The session entitled ‘Survival Strategies for Global Enterprises: Japan’s Toei on IP, Globalization, and Business Mindset’ took place as part of TCCF’s Forum section, which also includes sessions on Japan’s K2P Film Fund, Indonesian studio MD Entertainment’s scaling strategy, as well as panel discussions on co-production, mircodrama, AI adoption and IP exploitation. title: ‘Hold Onto Me,’ Cyprus’ First Oscar Hopeful, Stars a Newcomer and a ‘Dogtooth’ Actor in a Very Personal Father-Daughter Drama
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All November 6, 2026 9:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Hold Onto Me' Courtesy of PÖFF It’s summertime in Cyprus. Iris, 11, spends her days with her older best friend, Danae. But then she hears that her grandfather has died. Visiting town for his funeral is Iris’ father, Aris, whom she has never known. That is the starting point for Hold Onto Me , the feature debut of writer-director Myrsini Aristidou. Can Iris and Aris find a way to connect, even though he is a petty criminal and doesn’t want to take responsibility? Iris doesn’t give up and gets involved in his various schemes, despite warnings from her mother and her older brother. What begins as a stubborn attempt to reconnect slowly unfolds into a fragile bond. But then, Aris’ dark past gets them into trouble. Related Stories TV 'The Remarried Empress' Sets Disney+ and Hulu Record With Biggest Local Original Launch Ever Movies AFM Hot Project: Rosamund Pike to Star in Body Horror 'Feed' Hold Onto Me , starring newcomer Maria Petrova and Christos Passalis ( Dogtooth ), premiered at Sundance, where it won the World Cinema Dramatic Audience Award. It then became Cyprus’ first-ever international feature film Oscar submission. Now, the film screens in the Just Film youth and children’s event of the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival ( PÖFF ) in Estonia. Cercamon is handling sales. Lasse Ulvedal Tolbøll was the cinematographer on the Cyprus-Denmark-Greece co-production. The editors were Jenna Mangulad and Aristidou. Aristidou and Monica Nicolaidou produced the film, with Thomas J. Mangan IV and Mark Hollinger as the executive producers and Anders N.U. Berg, Konstantina Stavrianou and Rena Vougioukalou as co-producers. Watch a trailer for the film right here. Aristidou talked to THR about her bittersweet first feature, pairing an unknown as the young girl at the heart of it with the man who played the son in Dogtooth , her desire to make Hold Onto Me feel different and that first-ever Cypriot Oscar submission. The father-daughter theme is one that the filmmaker has also explored in two shorts. “I feel like this is like a triptych,” Aristidou tells THR . “My first short film called Semele in 2015 is also a father and daughter story and was the first time that I began exploring this theme. Then I did my second short film, Aria , which has a father daughter dynamic again, but with an older daughter – she’s a teenager. They were short, and I wanted to go deeper in this subject matter.” Hold Onto Me allowed her to do so in feature form, but she wanted it to be surprising and different from other films about similar familial relationships. “I wanted to use the archetypical relationship of father and daughter within a love story,” she explains. “It’s kind of a love story. It’s about two people who don’t know how to be together. They are sort of strangers in the beginning. They meet, then slowly come together, and they end up accepting each other or even loving each other in their own way. And when you set this up within the framework of a father, daughter and their family, it creates a different energy.” That is driven by societal expectations we have for family members. “When someone is your family, you are expected to love them, or you have more expectations than from just any stranger,” Aristidou highlights. “However, they are strangers. They have never really met or had any shared experiences. So this is the first time they are reconnecting, and I wanted to explore this.” The characters and story of Hold Onto Me keep developing as the movie unfolds, and that is by design. “On a first feature, it’s very easy to get very obsessed with what you want to do, so I was very tough on myself,” Aristidou tells THR . “When it comes to narrative structure and characters, I like to move the story forward in every scene. When I was writing, I was really thinking about that.” ‘Hold Onto Me’ Courtesy of PÖFF One key reason that the filmmaker has returned to father-daughter stories lies in her own life experience. “It’s very personal in many ways,” she shares. “My parents divorced when I was very young, and I was not really growing up with my dad. He wasn’t entirely gone like this character, but he was not that present. And he’s not a criminal but a writer. It was only when I turned 12 or 13 that we started having more of a relationship. And when I was 15, 16, we really bonded. We reached a point where we started talking about everything and we really forgave each other. We reconnected, and there was really an understanding and acceptance.” The film’s setting is also personal. Hold Onto Me was shot in Cyprus, and for the writer-director, it was particularly important to film near the sea. “I grew up near the sea, so there are references that are very personal,” Aristidou tells THR . “My dad used to have a small boat when I was a kid. I also always used to hang out with older kids because I had an older friend who was my best friend. There is a lot of truth in the film.” The chemistry between Iris and Aris in the film is palpable To ensure the right fit, casting took a lot of time. “We were shooting in July. Around April, I decided I was going to work with Christos,” the director recalls. She wanted to see him interact with different kids, most of them in Athens. The actor then went to Cyprus to meet the girl who ended up making the cut. “I saw Christos with Maria, and they felt family in a strange way,” Aristidou tells THR . “They phsically have things in common and look a bit like family. But Maria had zero experience. She had never done anything [in acting]. But I felt that there was something with them.” ‘Hold Onto Me’ Courtesy of PÖFF With the big casting decisions made, she was hoping to rehearse with the two leads, but that didn’t work out. “Christos was shooting something. And then, he got COVID, so he only arrived a day before the shoot,” she recalls. “We only read the script once, and then I just started shooting with both of them. So I just threw Maria into the wild with him. But I think it worked out perfectly because they didn’t know each other really – just like their characters.” The Oscar submission was, of course, special for the writer-director feel, especially since it’s the first for Cyprus. “It’s a big honor,” Aristidou shares. “I suddenly felt very responsible for my whole country. But in many ways, this film and I are carving this path for Cyprus. There was no film from Cyprus in Sundance before, and then we won an audience award. And then the Oscars . I guess it’s a new thing for everyone here and for me. So I’m learning a lot in the process. I know we’re a bit of the underdogs, but I’m trying to enjoy the ride.” So, what’s next for the filmmaker? “I really love this dynamic of strangers coming together and realizing how similar they are or bonding,” Aristidou says. “I don’t think I would do a father-daughter film again. But there’s something about this narrative arc that I really love. Actually, I’m trying to work on a TV show, which is a crime, spy thriller. But, let’s see. I’m working on a couple of things, and I’m reading a lot of scripts because my agents in the U.S. are sending a lot of scripts to read. So I’m also open to directing something I haven’t written.” THR

title: Stephen Chow Told Japan to Stop Aping Kung Fu, Says Boss of Film Fund Behind Kore-eda Hirokazu’s ‘Look Back’
full_text: × Nov 6, 2026 8:41pm PT Stephen Chow Told Japan to Stop Aping Kung Fu, Says Boss of Film Fund Behind Kore-eda Hirokazu’s ‘Look Back’ By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘3 Body Problem’ Director Derek Tsang Boards DEA True-Crime Series ‘Group 41’ From Zhang Yimou’s ‘Shadow’ Producer Jonah Greenberg (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago Stephen Chow Told Japan to Stop Aping Kung Fu, Says Boss of Film Fund Behind Kore-eda Hirokazu’s ‘Look Back’ 11 hours ago Why ‘Suits’ Japan Swapped Drugs for Cash: NBCUniversal, TBS Format Chiefs on Localizing Hits at Taiwan Creative Content Fest 13 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Naman Ramachandran Hong Kong star-director Stephen Chow once told K2 Pictures founder Kii Muneyuki that Japanese filmmakers should stop imitating kung fu and build action films on their own martial arts instead, Kii said Saturday at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. “He said, ‘You have karate, judo, jujitsu and kendo. That is Japanese culture. Only you can turn it into action films, so you should be the ones doing it. Stop aping kung fu,’” recalled Kii, who said he has shared drinks with Chow in Tokyo a few times. He added that he agreed with Chow, pointing to Netflix sumo drama “Sanctuary” as the kind of project that draws on culture unique to Japan. Related Stories Sundance Hires Tracy Brady as Marketing, Communications Chief Kii’s K2P Film Fund I, which backed Kore-eda Hirokazu’s “Look Back,” could also open its doors to new investors. The fund closed its $33 million equity round in February. Kii said more companies approached K2 about investing after the close, and that the round could reopen if existing backers agree. He has not yet decided whether to do so. Some 30 companies have invested so far, led by MUFG Bank, Japan’s biggest lender. Other backers include Bandai, Dentsu, the government-backed Development Bank of Japan and property companies Tokyu Land and Mori Trust. Kii serves as the fund’s general partner. TThe equity is being paired with loans that are being added one after another and will ultimately total $67 million, Kii said, for a planned total of $100 million and a target of 50 films over seven years. Kii shared the stage with director Nagata Koto, whose Fukushima-set noir “The Nuke Crab” K2 unveiled at Cannes in May. Kii said he and Nagata are aiming for a hit in Japan and in Eastern Europe, including Poland and Ukraine, where he believes audiences who lived through the Chernobyl accident might connect with it. The project is in development, with a shoot targeted for next year. The film follows those who profited from the huge sums that flowed from across Japan into the radiation clean-up of the Tohoku region. Nagata, whose “ Baka’s Identity ” competed at Busan last year, described the subject as socially taboo in Japan and the kind of material that productions involving TV networks or major studios would never take on. “When I took it to Kii-san, he immediately said, ‘That sounds interesting, let’s do it,’ and got it started,” Nagata said. Pairing Japan with one other specific market is a strategy K2 calls “Japan plus one.” “What Americans like about Japan, what the French like about Japan, what Taiwanese audiences like about Japan and what Koreans like about Japan are completely different,” Kii said. “The Japan that Japanese people like is different again.” Kii said that while the world knows about the Chernobyl disaster itself, far less is known about how the lives of people in the area changed afterward. Nagata said her goal is to secure international sales early enough that an overseas release can run alongside the Japanese one. She added that shared emotions such as friendship and family can make the unfamiliar feel closer. “I think jealousy and love are the same anywhere in the world, as long as we are human,” she said. K2 Pictures was set up as an alternative to Japan’s production committee system, under which films are made mainly with the local market in mind. Kii, who started out tearing tickets and making popcorn in cinemas before rising to producer at Toei, said the closed nature of that system kept out both foreign and outside investment, which in turn made it hard to share returns with creators. Profits at K2 are calculated title by title, with 70% going to investors and 30% to the creative side. “Producers and the people involved in making the film aren’t putting up money, but the film exists because of their creativity,” Kii said. The company completed six films this year, including “Look Back,” Kore-eda’s live-action adaptation of Fujimoto Tatsuki’s manga, which competed at Venice, and Son Myung-ah’s debut feature “Trophy,” which is due to open in Korea. Kii said the aim is six or seven releases a year, but admitted that a year in, the pace is “pretty tough.” K2 has opened outposts in Taiwan and Korea with the aim of distributing its films directly in both markets. Kii said 99.9% of Japan’s overseas film business consists of licensing deals, which he argued does little to raise the value of Japanese titles abroad. “Japanese people taking Japanese films to that place and promoting them hard there – I think that’s what raises their value,” he said. Greenlighting at K2 rests with its six or seven producers, Kii included, and he said he does not block a project a producer is set on. The only test is whether costs can be balanced against likely revenue. “Nobody can tell whether a film will be a hit,” Kii said. Kii said that applies equally to arthouse and commercial projects. “If it’s only going to bring in JPY50 million ($330,000), make it for JPY20 million ($130,000),” he said later in the session. The same logic applies to first-time directors. Kii said producers can line up pre-sales, streaming rights deals and sponsorships so that a debut cannot lose money, because a big loss makes it hard for a director to get a second film made. “I want to keep launching new directors from K2 Pictures,” Kii said. “And I want them to be grateful for the rest of their lives. Don’t forget us when you make it big.” Kii also wants the law changed. He said a British entertainment lawyer and an American completion bond executive both told him the film business works much like real estate: producers create assets and then turn them into cash. Japan passed an investment trust law around 2000 that lets real estate be securitized, but it does not cover content. Kii said he has been discussing the need for such a law with lawyers and hopes to push for one. title: After 2026 Midterms, Bill Maher Asks Trump, “Donnie, Are You OK?”
full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All November 6, 2026 8:29pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Bill Maher and President Donald Trump. Paul Morigi/Getty Images, Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images Logo text Bill Maher reacted to the 2026 midterm results during the Friday episode of Real Time , moreso reacting to President Donald Trump ‘s response to the election. During the host’s monologue, he said he predicted the midterms would be positive for Democrats. “Well, look, I hate to gloat, but sorry, I have to do a little bit because everybody was hedging about this election,” he said, as a montage of clips of him predicting the results was played. One thing Maher said he couldn’t have anticipated? Trump’s response to the results, he said. Related Stories TV The Other Midterms Flip: Broadcast Networks, Led by NBC, Dominated Election Night Coverage News Jimmy Kimmel, Seth Meyers Call Out Trump's "I Wasn't on the Ballot" Excuse for Midterm Losses: "Shut Up" “Here’s something I could not have predicted, which was Trump’s reaction to the election. He said, ‘Congratulations to the Democrats, they did a good job,'” Maher said wide-eyed, looking around at his Real Time audience. “Donnie, are you OK? I know we’ve been feuding. You sound unwell. You’re not even going to fake it was rigged?” He continued, “And let me tell you something, even with the attempted rigging — and they did try to rig it in every different kind of way; mail-in balloting, intimidating the voters, all that shit — democracy, man. Kind of fucking awesome.” During an interview with The New York Times shortly before 10:30 p.m. on Tuesday, the president said he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results. Trump added, “We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.” However, he also ranted about the midterms, writing on Truth Social that if he was on the ballot, “we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Maher’s comment about “feuding” with the president was likely a reference to their recent back-and-forth that was heightened after Trump penned a lengthy social media post where he slammed the comedian as a “complete and total loser,” and shared more details about their recent dinner at the White House. Maher responded to the rant during last week’s Oct. 30 episode of Real Time , joking that the president “went off on me like Kelly Clarkson in a toy store.” Elsewhere in the episode, the comedian said he thinks the president has been “amazingly humble” amid the results. “I thought by this time, he’d be suing the voters by name, individually, and arresting the poll workers. Instead, even he was like, ‘You know, even I’m sick of me a little bit.’” He joked that Trump saying he has “a lot of friends in the Democratic party” might open the door for him to visit the White House for a third time. “Wow, I might get to go again. Look at that,” he joked. THR

title: Taiwan’s Chunghwa Telecom Unveils 10 Content Investments, From ‘Gunshot’ to ‘Call of Lobster’
full_text: × Nov 6, 2026 7:36pm PT Taiwan’s Chunghwa Telecom Unveils 10 Content Investments, From ‘Gunshot’ to ‘Call of Lobster’ By Lin Ying-Hsuan Plus Icon Lin Ying-Hsuan Latest AI Filmmaking Platform Core Studio Launches at Taiwan Creative Content Fest With 24 Specialized Agents 7 hours ago Chang Chen Urges Emerging Taiwanese Actors to ‘Be Like Water’ at Taiwan Creative Content Fest Golden Horse Showcase 12 hours ago Taiwan Audience Study Highlights Cross-Platform IP Opportunities as AI Raises New Risks for Content Industry 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Chunghwa/TCCF Chunghwa Telecom , Taiwan’s largest telecom operator, announced 10 new investments at its “Chunghwa Telecom Content Slate and Partnership Showcase,” spanning film, TV and music projects as well as stakes in two production companies. The company pitched the slate as a way to back Taiwanese original IP and link local creators with partners abroad. The event was held at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF), which Chunghwa has sponsored for five consecutive years. Taiwan’s Minister of Culture Li Yuan attended, alongside Chunghwa chief business officer and senior executive VP Lin Wen-chiyh, consumer business group president Hu Hsueh-hai and representatives from the presenting teams. Related Stories Sundance Hires Tracy Brady as Marketing, Communications Chief “Chunghwa Telecom is like a pyramid,” Li said. “I am grateful that, beyond building a strong foundation through its thriving core business, the company is also willing to invest at the very top of the pyramid, supporting film and television professionals as they continue moving forward and creating even better work.” The slate includes four scripted series: police crime drama “Gunshot,” made with PTS Taigi TV, the Taiwanese-language channel of public broadcaster PTS, and S11 Partners; family fantasy “Yesterday’s Daughter, Tomorrow’s Mother,” from producer Phoebe Ma and director Hung Tzu-peng; fantasy adventure “Guides to the World Below,” adapted from a popular Taiwanese comic; and “C’est la Vie,” an urban drama about food and women’s personal growth, with actress Esther Liu as executive producer. Chunghwa has also invested in “Next Z Chef,” billed as Taiwan’s first cooking competition show for young people. Film investments include “Demon of the East: Black Condo,” a horror project tied to a cinematic universe that crosses four Asian countries, and “Call of Lobster,” which won the Chunghwa Telecom Award at TCCF’s 2024 pitching sessions and has since been selected for the Culture Ministry’s first international flagship cohort under its Great Voyage Project. The investments also extend to music, including “Speak in Silence,” an Asian tour by Taiwanese indie band Shallow Levée. The tour will run to about 50 shows in Taiwan and eight other countries across Asia. Alongside project financing, Chunghwa and Chunghwa Digital Cultural and Creative have taken equity positions in DaMou Entertainment and Horiza Creations. DaMou has produced series including “The World Between Us II” and “Wave Makers.” Horiza uses community engagement and crowdfunding to gauge what audiences want. “Chunghwa Telecom is more than just a platform operator; we are also a driving force behind the long-term development of the content industry,” Lin said. “Moving forward, we will continue to connect funding, creative talent, and domestic and international partners, leveraging our group’s resources and industry partnerships to help Taiwanese content reach international markets.” Chunghwa-backed films “Arrested Memory” and “The Photo From 1977” received a combined 12 nominations at the 63rd Golden Horse Awards. The company operates mobile and broadband networks as well as the MOD IPTV service and the Hami Video streaming platform, which together have more than 3 million subscribers. title: Netflix’s Radford Studio Acquisition Moving Ahead Despite Streamer’s Sunset Blvd Landlord Throwing Shade On Deal
full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Netflix’s Radford Studio Acquisition Moving Ahead Despite Streamer’s Sunset Blvd Landlord Throwing Shade On Deal Ken Ziffren Offers Optimistic View On Industry, Even When It Comes To AI & Federal Tax Credit Legislation Nithya Raman Wins L.A. Mayor Race As Karen Bass Concedes View All November 6, 2026 6:41pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Radford Studio Center Getty Images / Netflix Netflix didn’t end up owning the legendary Warner Bros lot after losing out earlier this year to David Ellison for the Burbank studio, but the streamer is still ploughing ahead to take control of Radford Studio Center in the next several months. Despite some recent shade thrown by Netflix’s current Sunset Blvd landlord, the long-rumored $400 million plus purchase of the 55-acre Studio City production facility by the Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters -run company is coming together on schedule. Netflix did not respond today to Deadline’s request for remarks on the status of the Radford acquisition. However, a source close to events said “the deal is progressing on the agreed upon timetable and with the agreed upon sets of milestone dates.” Related Stories Trailers 'The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth' Trailer: More Plot Details Emerge In Latest Look At Fincher-Tarantino-Pitt Team-Up Executives Emily Feingold Heads To Walt Disney As EVP Comms; Succeeds Retiring Studio Vet David Jefferson What exactly that timetable and those milestone dates are has been left vague. Late this summer, the streamer was granted more time to look into the bones of Radford and see what the true shape of the place is. Still, even with big layoffs, Peter Rice taking over as Content chief from the fired Bela Bajaria , declining engagement and an ailing stock (which dipped to $63.4 today), the desire at the upper echelon of Netflix for a sprawling studio lot of their own to cement the company’s industry dominance is stronger than ever. Watch on Deadline With Hudson Pacific CEO Victor Coleman announcing on a November 5 earnings call that Netflix “had not closed the transaction” on Radford, a real estate monsoon of sorts swelled up this week. Undercutting his own remarks, Coleman added, “they are not deciding to close it until sometime maybe later in the year, or not.” At present, there haven’t been any required filings with the SEC or L.A. County by Netflix for Radford Still, while the endgame has never really been in doubt since this summer, the fact is negotiations for Radford have been moving in ebbs and flow, I’m told. “They haven’t signed on the dotted line, that will all likely happen later this year,” a L.A. real estate insider added of where talks between Netflix and the Goldman Sachs-led group that took over the 98-year-old Radford when Hackman Capital Partners defaulted on a $1.1. billion loan early this year. “It’s a priority, sure. Remember with renovations and new builds, there’s a lot to put in place too.” (L-R) Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters, WBD CEO David Zaslav and Netflix-co-CEO Ted Sarandos tour the Warner Bros lot in late 2025 Joe Pugliese and John Nowak for Warner Bros. Discovery A December 17 stroll around the WB lot by Sarandos and Peters with then WBD CEO David Zaslav when the streamer looked certain to buy the joint wetted the Netflix’s CEO beaks. However, beyond those maters of the universe moments, it has also long been clear to Netflix’s execs that they needed a full service L.A. space of their own for both offices and production – which led to the start of talks with Goldman in April. As it is, the global HQ of the global streamer right now is a rented hodgepodge of Hudson Pacific-owned Sunset structures and venues that the Netflix has outgrown. With leases on the ICON building and others until 2031, Netflix is one of Hudson Pacific’s biggest customers. Netflix’s office building in Hollywood, California Robyn Beck/AFP via Getty Images Outside pricey California, Netflix has been building out from renter to owner itself the past few years. Leaning into incentives offered in other states, the streamer has Netflix Studios Albuquerque, a108-acre campus with 12 soundstages and more in New Mexico. In New York, there’s the six soundstages of Netflix Studios Brooklyn. Next door in New Jersey, the massive nearly 300-acre Netflix Studios Fort Monmouth studio is under construction at a cost of more than $1 billion. The projected 12 sound stages are expected to come online in staggered openings next year and in 2028. Add to all that, just outside London, the streamer’s UK hub of Longcross Studios with its five sound stages A CBS hub over the decades and once dubbed Republic Studios way back in the day, Radford has “22 stages, 210,000 square feet of office space and 172,737 square feet of support space,” according to its specs. The site of where Seinfeld, Gunsmoke , and The Mary Tyler Moore Show were shot, Radford has a number of current tenants who would obviously need to have their leases bought out if Netflix took over. After buying Radford in 2021 off what was then ViacomCBS for $1.85 bilion, Hackman and its partners planned to pour big bucks into upgrades and revamps. That all fell apart for the company, who own the likes of the 25-acre Television City on Fairfax and other venues around the world, as production in the home of Hollywood took a downward dive around 2023. Very quickly, once hard to get soundstage space became plentiful — and often empty.
